newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian ruling party heads for landslide win.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian ruling party heads for landslide win.

text.p: Indonesia's ruling Golkar party was cruising on Friday toward its forecast landslide win in general elections but attention was focused on the final margin of its victory and the size of a protest vote.

Thursday's elections were generally peaceful after a four-week campaign marked by the worst political violence in the country in more than three decades and rising dissent against the sometimes ruthless rule of President Suharto.

Political analysts have said there is no doubt that Golkar will win, given the tightly controlled political system in Indonesia, but added that the size of the majority could provide a pointer to Suharto's popularity.

At 3:30 a.m. (2030 GMT Thursday), election officials said some 59 million votes had been counted with Golkar winning 74.99 percent, the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) 22.29 percent and the divided Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) 2.72 percent.
Nearly 125 million people were eligible to vote and turnout in previous Indonesian elections has usually been around 90 percent, indicating more than half the ballots cast have been tallied.
Golkar won 68 percent of the vote at the last elections in 1992 and has set itself a target of over 70 percent this year. The PPP won 17 percent of the vote in 1992 and the PDI 15 percent.
"If it does worse than last time, Golkar will be seen to have failed," independent analyst Arief Budiman told Reuters recently.

Another analyst following the returns noted the steep fall in the PDI's vote and said the division in the party following the ouster of party chief Megawati Sukarnoputri by a government-backed faction last year was the cause.

Megawati, Indonesia's best-known opposition figure and the daughter of late founding president Sukarno, was barred from participating in the polls following her ouster. She said she would not vote in protest but stopped short of an illegal call for an election boycott.
Analysts have said a key figure to watch would be the number of votes returned blank or spoiled as a mark of protest, which would give some indication of support for Megawati.
That figure, reportedly around 3-4 percent at the last elections, is unlikely to be known until the government announces the complete results next week.
Police said at least 13 people were killed on Wednesday night in the troubled territory of East Timor as rebels tried to disrupt preparations for the poll.

A soldier was killed on Thursday in the former Portuguese colony while he was guarding a poll booth, police said. Indonesia annexed East Timor in 1976, a year after invading the territory, and a group of armed guerrillas still opposes Jakarta's rule in the territory.

One person was shot and killed during a gunfight between troops and Moslem fundamentalist rebels near a polling booth in Aceh province on Sumatra island on Thursday, the Jakarta Post newspaper reported.
Kompas newspaper also reported several minor poll violations, but analysts have said Indonesia's political system itself is slanted to ensure a Golkar victory.
All government servants are required to vote for Golkar and analysts have said development funds to villages that vote for minority parties mysteriously dry up.
Candidates for the polls are scrutinised by authorities beforehand and the minority parties are not allowed to question government policies during the campaign.
Despite the restrictions, the PPP attracted huge crowds during its campaign rallies, many of them supporters of Megawati, and freqent clashes broke out between its cadres and those of Golkar.

Analysts ascribed the violence to frustration among urban poor who have been left behind in the strong economic growth during Suharto's tenure but said it was unlikely to translate into a vote swing against Golkar.
